say: Welcome, Rate Racers! Today is about “how much for one”: one minute, one kilogram, one can. Once you know the rate for one, you can predict anything: how many pages in an hour, which pack is cheaper, when the tank will be full.
Shops, taps, printers and car parks all run on rates. By the end you will spot the trap in “Buy 10, get 2 free!”
Better Buy Showdown! Two packs of the same thing. Point left or right: which is the better buy? Then prove it.
Pens: 4 for $2.00, or 10 for $4.00. Point now. Who can prove it? Volunteers only, please. The price of ONE pen each time is the fair way to compare.
Printer A prints 72 pages in 4 minutes. Printer B prints 50 pages in 2 minutes. Which is faster? Now both print a 430-page job together. Guess the time before you work it out.
Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks, and before you touch the objects. Silent thinking. I will show the clock. Then talk with your partner.
stuck: Stuck: how many pages does each printer print in 1 minute? Start the table with 1 minute.
Not sure how to compare: “Compare the same number of minutes for both printers.”
If a pair wants more: how many pages should go to each printer so both finish at the same time?

say: “5 kg of rice cost $9.50. I want the price of 1 kg first: $9.50 ÷ 5 = $1.90. Now anything is easy: 3 kg is 3 × $1.90 = $5.70. And backwards: $13.30 is 1330 cents and 1 kg costs 190 cents, so 1330 ÷ 190 = 133 ÷ 19 = 7 kg.”
“Pens: 3 for $1.95 is 65¢ each. 5 for $3.10 is 62¢ each. So the 5-pack is the better buy, if I need that many. I check another way: 15 pens cost 5 × $1.95 = $9.75 or 3 × $3.10 = $9.30.”
“Two taps fill 9 ℓ and 6 ℓ each minute. Together, every minute, 15 ℓ go in. 180 ÷ 15 = 12 minutes. A leak takes out 3 ℓ a minute, so only 12 ℓ stay in each minute: 180 ÷ 12 = 15 minutes.”

do: Ask: “What is the rate for 1? One minute, one can, one kilogram?”
Ask: “How many cans do you really get in that deal?”
Ask: “Each minute, how much goes in and how much comes out?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Find the amount for 1 unit first.”
Hint 2: “Make a table: 1 minute, 2 minutes, 5 minutes … or draw a timeline.”
Hint 3: “Working together? Add the rates, not the times.”

Ask: “Each minute, how much goes in and how much comes out?”

say: “Is the biggest pack always the best buy? Give an example with numbers.”
“Where did you see a bigger pack that was NOT the better buy today?”
ask: “Is the biggest pack always the best buy? Give an example with numbers.”

No. Compare the price of 1: for example 3 pens for $1.95 is 65¢ a pen but 5 pens for $3.10 is 62¢ a pen (here the bigger pack is better); but if the 10-pack costs $7.50 and the 4-pack costs $2.80, the 4-pack is 70¢ a pen and the 10-pack is 75¢ a pen, so the small pack is the better buy. The better buy also depends on how many you really need.

say: “Today you found the rate for 1 and raced with it: scaling up, working backwards, adding taps together and catching the free-gift trap. Notice it, test it, explain why.”

p5l6-title.note: Minutes 0 to 2 (opening, inside the 90-minute clock). Objective: Find a rate for 1 unit and use it to scale up or work backwards in a rate table; compare buys by the price of one item (including a free-gift deal); add rates when taps or printers work together and take away a leak; work out charges "for every half hour or part of it"; and compare two price plans with a table. Thinking strategies taught today: FIND THE VALUE OF 1, MAKE A TABLE and PRETEND A NUMBER (taps that fill a tank in a stated time). Materials: mini whiteboards, a calculator for checking only, a stopwatch or phone, a few real price tags or supermarket flyers if you have them. Online: children write on whiteboards and say the answer together on three; the tutor fills the rate tables on the slides. Pairs work in breakout rooms for the Explore. The brain break uses a phone stopwatch. Time plan (the exact minutes of this lesson; every lesson adds up to 90): opening 0 to 2, sneak-peek puzzles 2 to 6 (one check for both puzzles, no volunteer round, nobody is marked), warm-up 6 to 12 (one game round, four quick questions), explore 12 to 26 (pair work 6 minutes at most, then two questions together; a Go further what-if is on the explore slide for any pair that finishes), teaching 26 to 38.5 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 38.5 to 42.5, workbook page 1 42.5 to 57 (the questions without a star; after question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder), check together 57 to 61, short teaching before page 2 61 to 62.5, workbook page 2 62.5 to 71.5 (alone: start with the questions named at the top, then choose; starred parts are take-home; nobody has to finish), check together 71.5 to 74.5, talk time 74.5 to 80 (you may say pass; volunteers first; the first step of the Investigation is take-home), exit ticket 80 to 85, reflection 85 to 87.5 (pass is always OK), stamp typed in the chat and goodbye 87.5 to 88.5, and the buffer 88.5 to 90 (floating time: spend it first if you run late, never fill it on purpose). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are open to every child and have no clock time. The tutor never announces who is on which page, and never splits a pair unless both children agree. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." SPINE: Today's tool is Make a table. Tabulate cases, find the change in each column, extend or generalise. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook.

p5l6-check.note: Minutes 2 to 6. SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES. Show puzzle 1 and give about a minute; click to show the short answer later. Then show puzzle 2 and give about a minute. Open with one line only: "Guessing is welcome. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is an access puzzle: any child can try it with objects, drawing or counting, so everyone can start well. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. ONE check for both puzzles: after puzzle 2, everyone says the answers together on three (face to face, you may glance at papers held low as you walk round; online, nothing is held up to the camera). Then click through the two short answers and say each with one short reason. NO volunteer round here (volunteers come in the talk time). Never boards in front of the group, never read out answers with names, no tally, no ranking. Never record scores. Answers and what to listen for. Q1: 3 litres each minute, so 18 litres in 6 minutes (6 × 3).; Q2: Mei. Ali reads 3 pages a minute (12 ÷ 4) and Mei reads 4 pages a minute (20 ÷ 5). Comparing the amount for 1 minute makes it fair. SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES (about 4 minutes). Show the two puzzles one at a time. Say one line only: "Guessing is welcome. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is one that any child can try with objects, drawing or counting, so everybody can start well. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. Answers are shown PRIVATELY, never on boards in front of the group. Face to face: children write on their own paper and show it only to you as you walk round. Online: children say the answers together on three; nothing is held up to the camera. Do not read answers out with names, do not keep a tally, do not rank. Use ONE check for both puzzles (after puzzle 2, everyone says the answers together on three), then click through the answers and say each one with one short reason. There is NO volunteer round in the sneak-peek; volunteers come in the talk time. Never choose a child because you saw a wrong answer. Never record scores. Choosing a start: every child has the same neutral line on workbook page 1: "After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." (The number is the last question on page 1 of this lesson.) Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Never single out a child by name and never announce who is on which page. Pairs are not split unless BOTH children agree. Any child may swap at any time.

p5l6-warm1.note: Minutes 6 to 8.5. Better Buy Showdown, whole numbers only so that everyone can start. Children point left or right (online: hold up a left or right hand), then you click to show the proof. Pens: 4 for $2.00 is 50 cents each; 10 for $4.00 is 40 cents each, so the 10-pack. Then the two questions: Ali needs only 4 pens, so he buys the 4-pack ($2.00 against $4.00 for 10); the price of one is the fair way to compare. TUTOR EXTENSION, only if the group is ready (these need decimal division): Juice: $3.00 / 1.5 = $2.00 a litre; $3.80 / 2 = $1.90 a litre, so the 2 litre bottle. Eggs: $3.20 / 10 = 32 cents each; $3.96 / 12 = 33 cents each, so the 10-pack (the bigger pack is NOT cheaper per egg). Ask: "Why is it fair to compare the price of ONE?" Watch for children who compare the pack prices ($2.40 and $3.80). Do not say "the bigger pack is always better": the eggs show it is not.

p5l6-warm2.note: Minutes 8.5 to 12. Read each aloud, write it, say the answer together on three, then click to show. Answers: $2.50, 180 pages, 150 ml, $12. If you are short of time, skip question 4. After 2 ask: "Which operation scales up?" (multiply). After 4 ask: "How many 100 g are in 1 kg?" (10, so multiply the price by 10).

p5l6-explore1.note: Minutes 12 to 26 (the whole explore; this slide 12 to 22). Pairs build a rate table for each printer. Ask them to predict first: which is faster, and how long for the 430-page job together? Many say A, because 72 is more than 50. Let them test it: in 4 minutes A prints 72 pages but B prints 100. Hint: how many pages in 1 minute? Pair work is at most 6 minutes: the 430-page job (how long do both printers together take?) is the Go further what-if, not part of the pair task. Anyone who wants more (open to every pair): how long do both printers together take for 430 pages (10 minutes), and how many pages should go to each so both finish at the same time? (A 180, B 250: 10 minutes each.) PROTECTED THINK TIME: before the pairs touch anything, say "Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks" and show the clock; then pairs talk and start. PAIR WORK IS CAPPED AT 6 MINUTES: say "Pencils down" at minute 22 and bring the group back (the minutes before that include the 30 seconds of thinking, finding materials and, in lessons that use them, the move to and from breakout rooms). GO FURTHER (say it as soon as a pair has finished the task): any pair that finishes early may try the what-if question on the next slide. It is open to every pair, not a reward. Answer: 10 minutes (18 + 25 = 43 pages a minute; 430 ÷ 43 = 10). Printer A gets 180 pages (18 × 10) and printer B gets 250 pages (25 × 10); 180 + 250 = 430. If both work for the whole 10 minutes they finish together.

p5l6-explore2.note: Minutes 22 to 26. Pencils down: gather the pairs. Answers: 1) B is faster: 25 pages a minute against 18 pages a minute for A (or compare 4 minutes: A 72, B 100). (Go further, not asked together: together 18 + 25 = 43 pages a minute, and 430 / 43 = 10 minutes. Children who guessed "add the times" (4 + 2 = 6) will need the teaching slides.) 2) With the rate for 1 minute we can compare fairly, multiply to scale up and divide to find a time. Do not give the method if nobody finds it: the later slides teach it. TWO questions together only (about a minute each), then move on. GO FURTHER what-if (open to every pair as soon as it has finished; nobody waits): 10 minutes (18 + 25 = 43 pages a minute; 430 ÷ 43 = 10). Printer A gets 180 pages (18 × 10) and printer B gets 250 pages (25 × 10); 180 + 250 = 430. If both work for the whole 10 minutes they finish together.

p5l6-teach1.note: Minutes 26 to 28. Teach. Fill the table with the children. Ask first: "What do we need to know to get 3 kg?" (the price of 1 kg). Click step 1: 9.50 / 5 = 1.90. Click step 2: 3 x 1.90 = 5.70. Check another way: 3 kg is 3/5 of 5 kg, 3/5 of 9.50 is 5.70. Click step 3: change dollars to cents first, 1330 / 190 = 133 / 19 = 7 kg. Children who prefer can test it: 7 x $1.90 = $13.30. Think-aloud: "A rate is how much for ONE. Once I know the rate for one, everything else is multiply or divide." Use a real price tag if you have one. The rate for 1 minute, 1 kg, 1 can are all the same idea.

p5l6-we1.note: Minutes 28 to 30. Click to reveal the price of 1 pen, then the steps. Think-aloud: "To compare fairly I need the same unit: the price of ONE pen. 195 cents divided by 3 is 65. 310 cents divided by 5 is 62. 62 is smaller, so the 5-pack is cheaper per pen." Check another way: buy 15 pens each way (the common multiple of 3 and 5): 5 packs of 3 cost 5 x 1.95 = 9.75; 3 packs of 5 cost 3 x 3.10 = 9.30. Same answer. Last box: the better buy per pen is not always the one you should buy; you may not need that many.

p5l6-try1.note: Minutes 30 to 31.5. Write it, say the answer together on three, then click. a) $3.20 / 4 = 80 cents each; 7 x 80 = $5.60. b) 135 / 15 = 9. (Two items only.)

p5l6-teachfree.note: Minutes 31.5 to 33.5. Teach before worksheet page 1 (Q2, shop C has a free-gift deal). Ask first: "Do you pay for the free pencils?" (No, but you get them, so they share the price.) Click through. Think-aloud: "I pay $4 and I walk away with 10 pencils. $4 divided by 10 is 40 cents." The trap: dividing by 8 gives 50 cents and the wrong shop. Check: 20 pencils from shop A cost 2 x $4 = $8; 20 pencils from shop B cost 4 x $2.25 = $9.

p5l6-we2.note: Minutes 33.5 to 35.5. Click to build the table row by row. Think-aloud: "Every minute tap A puts in 9 and tap B puts in 6, so 15 go in every minute. How many 15s make 180? 12 minutes. The crack lets out 3 every minute, so only 12 stay. How many 12s make 180? 15 minutes." Stress: we add RATES (litres a minute), never times. A common mistake is to say "A takes 20 minutes and B takes 30, so together 50". Together must be faster than either tap alone. Ask: "Is 12 minutes sensible? Tap A alone would need 180 / 9 = 20 minutes, so 12 is faster, good."

p5l6-try2.note: Minutes 35.5 to 37. Whiteboards. a) 8 + 12 = 20 ℓ a minute; 200 / 20 = 10. b) 25 + 15 = 40 pages a minute; 480 / 40 = 12. (Two items only.)

p5l6-key.note: Minutes 37 to 38.5. Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Adding or averaging the times when taps or printers work together (20 minutes and 30 minutes gives 50 or 25) instead of adding the rates. (2) Choosing the better buy by the pack price, or dividing a free-gift deal by the cans paid for instead of all the cans received. (3) Charges "for every half hour or part of it": dividing exactly instead of rounding up to the next half hour, or charging the first hour twice.

p5l6-break.note: Minutes 38.5 to 42.5. Use a phone stopwatch. One round only: 60 seconds of star jumps; children count once and say the number. Ask: "Would your rate be the same for 10 seconds? For an hour?" (we get tired: a rate stays the same only if the speed stays the same, which machines do and people do not).

p5l6-ws1.note: Minutes 42.5 to 57. Walk around. Ask "What is the rate for 1?" and "How many cans do you really get in that deal?" before giving any help. (Ben needing exactly 20 cans from more than one shop is in the Think harder pool: try whole packs that make exactly 20.) Q3 (b) (c) and (d) are take-home (starred); do not wait for them. Everyone sees the same neutral line: "After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." (Question 3 is the last question to do in class on page 1 of this lesson.) Never announce who is on which page and never name a child in front of the group. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Do not split a pair unless BOTH children agree. Think harder is the next pages after the Investigation page in the workbook. IN CLASS NOW: Q1 (a) (b), Q2 (the Start-here line, (a) (b)) and Q3 (a). Parts marked with a star in the workbook are take-home: say so once ("the starred parts are for home") and do not wait for them.

p5l6-ws1ans.note: Minutes 57 to 61. One pair explains Q2 (the heaviest); click through the rest (Q3 (b) (c) are take-home, their answers are here for you). Click each answer after a pair explains theirs. Q1: 48 / 3 = 16 bottles a minute; 5 minutes 80; 160 bottles take 10 minutes; 12 minutes 192. Q1b: 400 / 16 = 25 minutes, so 9.25 a.m. Q2a: $4.20 / 6 = 70 cents; $2.92 / 4 = 73 cents; shop C gives 12 cans for $7.80: 65 cents. Extra (Think harder pool): 20 cans exactly, any correct way is fine. One deal from C (12 cans, $7.80) and two packs from B (8 cans, $5.84) = $13.64 (the cheapest). Two packs from A and two from B = $8.40 + $5.84 = $14.24. Five packs from B = $14.60. Compare two ways. (The cheapest for at least 20 cans is on the Go further page: 22 cans cost $14.92 and 24 cans cost $15.60.) Q3: a) 240 / 12 = 20; b) 240 / 30 = 8; c) 30 - 6 = 24 a minute, 240 / 24 = 10;

p5l6-teachplans.note: Minutes 61 to 62.5. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q6). Ask first: "Which plan do you think is cheaper?" Take a show of hands, then test with a table. Click the rows. Think-aloud: "For each number of visits I work out both costs. At 4 visits Plan A costs 24 + 12 = 36 and B costs 20. At 12 visits they are both 60. After 12 visits B is dearer." Why 12? Each visit costs Plan B $2 more than Plan A, and Plan A starts $24 higher, so they meet after 24 / 2 = 12 visits. The table tells us WHEN the answer changes: it depends on how many visits you will make. Use a table, not algebra.

p5l6-ws2.note: Minutes 62.5 to 71.5. Children work alone on Q4 (a) (b) and Q6 (a); Q5 and Q6 (b) (c) are take-home (starred). Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson, especially children who still add the times for taps or printers. Page 2 is a menu, not a wall. Everyone sees the same line: start with Q4 (a) (b) and Q6 (a), then choose. Nobody has to finish; stop at minute 71.5 whatever has been done, because the check-together slide gives every answer with its explanation. Starred parts are take-home (their answers are on the check slide for you; do not spend class time on them). Walk round, ask "what could you try first?", and give the first hint before any answer.

p5l6-ws2ans.note: Minutes 71.5 to 74.5. One child explains Q4; click through the rest (Q5 and Q6 (b) (c) are take-home, their answers are here for you). Click each answer after a child explains. Q4a: 30 + 20 = 50 pages a minute; 900 / 50 = 18. Q4b: P alone prints 150 pages in 5 minutes; 750 left; 750 / 50 = 15; 5 + 15 = 20 minutes. Think harder pool (splitting 900 pages): both finish in 18 minutes; P prints 30 x 18 = 540 and Q prints 20 x 18 = 360. Q5a: 9.40 a.m. to 1.15 p.m. is 3 h 35 min; after the first hour 155 min = 5 half hours + 5 min, so 6 lots: $1.20 + 6 x 60 cents = $4.80. Q6c: 14 visits: A $30 + $56 = $86; B $98.

p5l6-stretch.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Think harder questions A1 to A4 (the same as the workbook). Answers: A1) 5 ℓ a minute (the tank holds 180 ℓ; 180 ÷ 9 = 20 ℓ a minute together; 20 − 15 = 5) A2) $9.60 (one box of 10 and three boxes of 6 make 28 eggs; three boxes of 10 cost $9.90) A3) $9.50 (4 h 35 min: first hour, then 3 h 35 min is 8 half hours or parts) A4) 100 minutes (Plan B costs 15¢ more each minute; $15 ÷ 15¢ = 100; both cost $25)

p5l6-stretch2.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Think harder questions A1 to A4 (the same as the workbook). Answers: A1) 5 ℓ a minute (the tank holds 180 ℓ; 180 ÷ 9 = 20 ℓ a minute together; 20 − 15 = 5) A2) $9.60 (one box of 10 and three boxes of 6 make 28 eggs; three boxes of 10 cost $9.90) A3) $9.50 (4 h 35 min: first hour, then 3 h 35 min is 8 half hours or parts) A4) 100 minutes (Plan B costs 15¢ more each minute; $15 ÷ 15¢ = 100; both cost $25)

p5l6-gofurther.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Go further questions B1 to B3 (the same as the workbook). Answers: B1) 3 cats (each cat eats 1 fish every 3 minutes, so the 3 cats eat 1 fish a minute: 100 fish in 100 minutes) B2) After 6 hours, both 8 cm tall (the gap of 6 cm closes by 1 cm each hour) B3) 30 minutes (pretend the bath holds 60 ℓ: 5 ℓ a minute in, 3 ℓ a minute out, 2 ℓ a minute stay: 60 ÷ 2) Make up your own (printed under Go further): Make up a better-buy puzzle with three packs of the same thing. Which pack is the best buy? Swap and check. Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks. Open-ended: check that a partner can solve it and that exactly one answer fits.

p5l6-gofurther2.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Go further questions B1 to B3 (the same as the workbook). Answers: B1) 3 cats (each cat eats 1 fish every 3 minutes, so the 3 cats eat 1 fish a minute: 100 fish in 100 minutes) B2) After 6 hours, both 8 cm tall (the gap of 6 cm closes by 1 cm each hour) B3) 30 minutes (pretend the bath holds 60 ℓ: 5 ℓ a minute in, 3 ℓ a minute out, 2 ℓ a minute stay: 60 ÷ 2) Make up your own (printed under Go further): Make up a better-buy puzzle with three packs of the same thing. Which pack is the best buy? Swap and check. Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks. Open-ended: check that a partner can solve it and that exactly one answer fits.

p5l6-challenge.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. These are in the question bank. Answers: 1) 10.15 a.m. (400 cups by 10.00; then 80 cups a minute; 1200 / 80 = 15 minutes more). 2) 30 minutes (pretend the bath holds 60 litres: 5 litres a minute in, 3 a minute out, 2 a minute stay in: 60 / 2 = 30). Many children say 8 minutes (20 - 12) or 32: pretending a number shows why they are wrong. 3) Neither. Together the taps must be faster than the faster tap alone, so the answer is less than 20 minutes. Pretend the tank holds 60 litres (both 20 and 30 go into 60): tap A fills 3 litres a minute and tap B fills 2, together 5 litres a minute, and 60 / 5 = 12 minutes.

p5l6-chdiag.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Show after pairs have tried Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: What do you notice? In E1, how many cups does machine 1 make before machine 2 starts? Which rate applies after 10.00? In B3, how much water goes in and how much goes out each minute? Which number could we pretend the bath holds? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p5l6-chwalk.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Use after pairs have tried. E1: split into two stages: machine 1 alone for 8 minutes, then both machines. B3: nobody told us how big the bath is, so we PRETEND: choose a number that both 12 and 20 divide into (60, the smallest, works). The answer does not depend on the pretend number: try 120 litres: 10 in, 6 out, 4 stay, 120 / 4 = 30 minutes again.

p5l6-talk.note: Minutes 74.5 to 80. Pairs talk for 2 minutes, then share. Answer: no. Compare the price of 1. Example: 3 pens for $1.95 is 65 cents a pen and 5 pens for $3.10 is 62 cents a pen, so here the bigger pack is better. But 4 pens for $2.80 is 70 cents a pen and 10 pens for $7.50 is 75 cents a pen, so the small pack is the better buy. The better buy also depends on how many you really need (if Mei needs only 3 pens, the 3-pack costs less). Second question if time: "Where did the eggs in the warm-up show this?" Praise the reasons, not only the answers. Protected think time: before anyone speaks, everyone thinks silently for 30 seconds (show the clock). Then pairs talk. This applies to the explore, to the talk question and to any make-up-your-own prompt. The Investigation first step is take-home (or the opener of the next lesson): tell the group so at the end of the talk time. Talk-time rules: say "You may say pass." Ask for VOLUNTEERS first, then invite others only if they want to. No cold-calling by name, no public tallies or rankings, and no "who got it right?" hands. Talk time: 30 seconds of silent thinking, 2 minutes pairs talk, 1 and a half minutes volunteers share, then tell everyone that the first step of the Investigation (the page after workbook page 2) is take-home, or the opener of the next lesson. Pass is always allowed.

p5l6-exit.note: Minutes 80 to 85. Answers: 8 minutes (15 + 10 = 25 ℓ a minute; 200 / 25 = 8). With the crack, 10 minutes (25 - 5 = 20 ℓ a minute; 200 / 20 = 10). Extension: make a better-buy poster of three pack sizes where the biggest pack is NOT the best buy. Swap with a partner.

p5l6-reflect.note: SPINE: Minutes 85 to 87.5. Start the timer (75 seconds). Say: "Pick one problem from today. Question 1: did I answer the question? Question 2: does my answer make sense? Question 3: can I check it another way? Tick, write one line, or pass. If you are still stuck, tick the box and I will come." Children tick the Look back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook, or just tick on paper. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share. Praise a check you saw, not speed. Then stamp the journals. After the look-back, minutes 87.5 to 90 are flex time (the buffer): finish stamps, then goodbye. Do not start anything new.
